stem: According to the source, why was the Nile flood important for farmers in ancient Egypt? Give two reasons.
source: Every year in ancient Egypt, the River Nile flooded between July and September. When the water went down, it left behind a layer of thick black mud called silt. Farmers planted their seeds in this rich soil in the autumn. They grew wheat to make bread and barley to make beer. They also grew flax, which was used to make linen cloth. Because the soil was so dark, the Egyptians called their land Kemet, which means "the black land". The desert around the valley was called Deshret, "the red land", because almost nothing could grow there. Farmers dug small canals to carry water to fields that were further from the river. Without the flood, Egypt would have had very little food.
points: When the flood went down it left rich black mud (silt) in which farmers planted their seeds
The flood made it possible to grow crops such as wheat and barley; without it Egypt would have had very little food
model_answer: The flood was important because when the water went down it left thick black mud called silt, and farmers planted their seeds in this rich soil. This let them grow wheat, barley and flax, and without the flood Egypt would have had very little food.

stem: Using the source, describe where Wadi Nakhl is and explain why most houses are on the eastern bank of the river.
source: Wadi Nakhl is a small town in the south of the country of Samara. It lies in a narrow valley between two lines of rocky hills. A small river called the Nakhl runs through the middle of the town from north to south. Most houses are built on the eastern bank of the river because the western bank floods in winter. The town is famous for its palm trees, which grow along both banks. There is one main road. It runs along the river and connects Wadi Nakhl with the coastal city of Bahriya, 60 kilometres to the north. In summer the weather is very hot and dry, so people often work early in the morning and rest in the afternoon.
points: Wadi Nakhl is in the south of Samara, in a narrow valley between rocky hills
Most houses are on the eastern bank because the western bank floods in winter
model_answer: Wadi Nakhl is a small town in the south of Samara, in a narrow valley between two lines of rocky hills. Most houses are on the eastern bank of the river because the western bank floods in winter.

stem: According to the source, who built the Great Pyramid, and what shows that the workers were treated well? Give three points.
source: The Great Pyramid at Giza was built for King Khufu about 4,500 years ago. For a long time people believed it was built by slaves, but archaeologists have found the remains of a workers' village near the pyramids. The workers lived in houses there, ate bread, fish and meat, and received medical care when they were hurt. Some workers were skilled builders who worked all year. Others were farmers who came to work for a few months while the Nile flood covered their fields and they could not farm. The huge stone blocks were cut with copper tools and moved on wooden sledges. Workers poured water on the sand in front of the sledges to make them slide more easily. When a worker died, he was buried in a tomb close to the pyramid, which shows that the workers were respected.
points: It was built by skilled builders and by farmers who worked during the flood, not by slaves
The workers lived in a village near the pyramids, ate bread, fish and meat, and got medical care when hurt
Workers who died were buried in tombs close to the pyramid, which shows they were respected
model_answer: The Great Pyramid was not built by slaves but by skilled builders who worked all year and by farmers who came while the flood covered their fields. The workers lived in a village near the pyramids, ate bread, fish and meat, and received medical care when they were hurt. When a worker died he was buried in a tomb close to the pyramid, which shows that the workers were respected.

stem: According to the source, how is a class representative chosen at Al-Amal Primary School, and what is one duty of a representative?
source: At Al-Amal Primary School, every class chooses one pupil to sit on the school council. Pupils who want to be chosen give a short speech to their class. Then every pupil writes one name on a piece of paper and puts it in a box. This is called a secret vote, because nobody sees what you write. The pupil with the most votes becomes the class representative. The council meets with the head teacher once a month. Representatives share their classmates' ideas, for example asking for more shade in the playground or a reading corner in the library. Last year the council asked for water coolers on every floor, and the school agreed. Representatives must listen to all pupils in their class, not only their friends.
points: Candidates give a speech, then the class holds a secret vote and the pupil with the most votes wins
A representative shares classmates' ideas at council meetings and must listen to all pupils, not only friends
model_answer: Pupils who want to be representative give a short speech, then everyone writes one name on a paper in a secret vote, and the pupil with the most votes wins. One duty of a representative is to listen to all pupils in the class, not only friends, and share their ideas at the council.

stem: According to the source, how can farmers grow crops in Bir Saba when it almost never rains? Give two details.
source: The Bir Saba oasis lies in the Western Desert, far from the Nile. Rain almost never falls there; in some years there is no rain at all. Even so, the oasis is green, because water comes up from under the ground. This underground water fell as rain thousands of years ago and was trapped in layers of rock. Today farmers reach it by digging wells. They use the water to grow date palms, olives and vegetables. Because the summer days are extremely hot, farmers plant vegetables in the shade of the tall palm trees. At night the desert becomes cold, because there are no clouds to keep the heat in. The people of Bir Saba must use water carefully, since the underground water is not being refilled by new rain.
points: They use underground water, trapped in the rock from ancient rain, which they reach by digging wells
They plant vegetables in the shade of the tall palm trees to protect them from the extreme heat
model_answer: Farmers in Bir Saba use underground water that fell as rain thousands of years ago and was trapped in rock; they reach it by digging wells. They also plant their vegetables in the shade of the tall palm trees because the summer days are extremely hot.

stem: According to the source, describe three reforms Muhammad Ali made to make Egypt strong.
source: Muhammad Ali became ruler of Egypt in 1805. He wanted Egypt to be strong and independent, so he began many changes. First, he built a large modern army and brought in European officers to train it. To supply the army, he opened factories that made cloth, guns and ships. Second, he took control of most of the farmland and told farmers which crops to grow. He encouraged long-staple cotton, which sold for high prices in Europe, and the money paid for his projects. Third, he sent groups of young Egyptians to study in France and opened new schools, including schools of medicine and engineering. These reforms made Egypt stronger, but they were hard on ordinary farmers, who paid heavy taxes and were forced to serve in the army or work on canals.
points: He built a large modern army trained by European officers and opened factories to supply it
He took control of farmland and encouraged long-staple cotton, whose sale in Europe paid for his projects
He sent young Egyptians to study in France and opened new schools such as medicine and engineering
model_answer: First, Muhammad Ali built a large modern army trained by European officers and opened factories making cloth, guns and ships to supply it. Second, he took control of the farmland and encouraged long-staple cotton, which sold for high prices in Europe and paid for his projects. Third, he sent young Egyptians to study in France and opened new schools of medicine and engineering.

stem: According to the source, give one rule that citizens of Kafr Salam must follow and one duty of the town council.
source: In the town of Kafr Salam, water is scarce in summer. The town council made new rules to make sure every family has enough. Gardens may only be watered after sunset, when less water is lost to the heat. Washing cars with a hose is not allowed; people must use a bucket instead. Every house now has a water meter, and families who use much more than the average pay a higher price. The council also has duties: it must repair broken pipes within two days and tell people in advance if the water will be cut. Citizens can report leaks by calling a free number. The mayor said, "Water belongs to all of us, so saving it is everyone's duty."
points: A citizens' rule: water gardens only after sunset, or wash cars with a bucket instead of a hose
A council duty: repair broken pipes within two days, or warn people in advance before the water is cut
model_answer: One rule is that citizens may only water their gardens after sunset. One duty of the council is to repair broken pipes within two days.

stem: According to the source, why was the Suez Canal important for world trade, and what did it cost Egypt? Give three points.
source: The Suez Canal was opened in November 1869. It joined the Mediterranean Sea to the Red Sea, so ships travelling between Europe and Asia no longer had to sail all the way around Africa. This made the journey from Britain to India thousands of kilometres shorter. The canal was planned by the French engineer Ferdinand de Lesseps and was dug over about ten years. Tens of thousands of Egyptian workers were forced to dig it, and many died from heat, disease and hard work. Egypt also paid a large part of the cost and fell deeply into debt. In 1875 the ruler Khedive Ismail had to sell Egypt's shares in the canal to Britain. Britain's interest in the canal later became one reason for its occupation of Egypt in 1882.
points: It joined the Mediterranean and the Red Sea, so ships between Europe and Asia no longer sailed around Africa
Tens of thousands of Egyptian workers were forced to dig it and many died
Egypt paid much of the cost, fell into debt and had to sell its canal shares to Britain in 1875
model_answer: The Suez Canal joined the Mediterranean Sea to the Red Sea, so ships between Europe and Asia no longer had to sail around Africa, making the journey thousands of kilometres shorter. But tens of thousands of Egyptian workers were forced to dig it and many died. Egypt also paid a large part of the cost, fell into debt and in 1875 had to sell its shares to Britain.

stem: Using the source, explain why rainforests are important for the planet and why cutting them down causes damage. Give three points.
source: Tropical rainforests grow near the equator, where it is hot all year and rain falls almost every day. The Amazon rainforest in South America is the largest in the world. A rainforest has layers. The tallest trees form the emergent layer. Below them is the canopy, a thick roof of leaves where most animals live. Very little sunlight reaches the forest floor, so few plants grow there. Rainforests are important for the whole planet. Their trees take in carbon dioxide and give out oxygen, and they are home to more than half of the world's kinds of plants and animals. However, large areas are being cut down to make space for cattle farms and to sell the wood. When the trees are removed, heavy rain washes the thin soil away.
points: The trees take in carbon dioxide and give out oxygen
Rainforests are home to more than half of the world's kinds of plants and animals
When the trees are cut down, heavy rain washes the thin soil away
model_answer: Rainforests are important because their trees take in carbon dioxide and give out oxygen, and they are home to more than half of the world's kinds of plants and animals. Cutting them down causes damage because, once the trees are gone, heavy rain washes the thin soil away.

stem: According to the source, how did the council of Nazlet Omar make its decision, and what did it decide?
source: The village council of Nazlet Omar had money for only one new project this year. Some members wanted to repair the road to the market, which becomes muddy and dangerous in winter. Others wanted to build a small health clinic, because the nearest doctor is 15 kilometres away. Before deciding, the council held an open meeting in the youth centre. More than two hundred villagers came and gave their opinions. Many mothers said that sick children could not reach the doctor quickly. Farmers said that bad roads damaged their vegetables on the way to market. In the end the council voted seven to four for the clinic, and promised to look for money for the road next year. The council published its decision and the reasons on the noticeboard of the mosque and the school.
points: The council held an open meeting where villagers gave their opinions, and then the council voted
It decided (seven votes to four) to build the health clinic and promised to look for money for the road next year
model_answer: Before deciding, the council held an open meeting in the youth centre where more than two hundred villagers gave their opinions, and then the members voted. They decided, seven votes to four, to build the health clinic and promised to look for money for the road next year.

stem: According to the source, why was the Rosetta Stone so important for understanding hieroglyphs?
source: In 1799, French soldiers in Egypt found a large dark stone near the town of Rashid, which Europeans called Rosetta. The stone carried the same message written three times: in hieroglyphs, in demotic, which was an everyday Egyptian script, and in ancient Greek. Scholars could already read ancient Greek, so they knew what the message said. This gave them a key to the hieroglyphs, which nobody had been able to read for more than a thousand years. In 1822 the French scholar Jean-François Champollion announced that he had understood how hieroglyphs worked. He had also studied Coptic, a late form of the Egyptian language, which helped him. After his discovery, scholars could read the writing on temples, tombs and papyri.
points: The same message was written three times: in hieroglyphs, demotic and ancient Greek
Scholars could already read Greek, so it gave them a key to the hieroglyphs, which Champollion understood in 1822
model_answer: The Rosetta Stone carried the same message in hieroglyphs, demotic and ancient Greek. Because scholars could already read Greek, they knew what the message said, and this gave them a key to the hieroglyphs, which Champollion understood in 1822.

stem: Using the source, explain why people in Lunara move to cities and describe two problems this movement causes.
source: In the country of Lunara, the number of people living in cities has grown quickly. In 1980 only one person in four lived in a city; today more than half do. Most newcomers move from villages to the capital, Port Selin. Young people leave the countryside because farms are small and droughts have made farming less reliable. In the city they hope to find jobs in factories, shops and building work, and to study at the university. This movement has brought problems. Housing is expensive, so many families live in crowded areas at the edge of the city, often without clean water. Traffic jams are common. Meanwhile, many villages now have mostly older people and children, and some fields are no longer farmed.
points: They leave villages because farms are small and droughts have made farming less reliable
They hope to find jobs in factories, shops and building work, and to study at the university
Two problems, e.g. expensive housing so families live in crowded edge areas without clean water; traffic jams; villages left with old people and children and unfarmed fields
model_answer: People leave the villages of Lunara because farms are small and droughts have made farming less reliable, and they hope to find jobs in factories, shops and building work or to study at the university in Port Selin. One problem is that housing is expensive, so many families live in crowded areas at the edge of the city without clean water. Another is that villages are left with mostly older people and children, and some fields are no longer farmed.

stem: According to the source, what travelled along the Silk Road besides goods? Give two examples.
source: The Silk Road was not one road but a network of trade routes that linked China with Central Asia, Persia, Arabia and the Mediterranean. It was used for more than a thousand years. Few merchants travelled the whole way. Instead, goods passed from trader to trader, and their price rose at every stop. From China came silk, paper and porcelain. From the west came glass, wool, gold and silver. Camels carried loads across the deserts, and travellers rested in roadside inns called caravanserais. Ideas travelled too. Religions such as Buddhism spread along the routes, and Chinese papermaking slowly reached the Middle East and later Europe. Sadly, diseases also travelled with the traders.
points: Religions, such as Buddhism, spread along the routes
Knowledge such as the Chinese skill of papermaking reached the Middle East and Europe (diseases also travelled)
model_answer: Besides goods, ideas travelled along the Silk Road. Religions such as Buddhism spread along the routes, and the Chinese skill of papermaking reached the Middle East and later Europe. Diseases also travelled with the traders.

stem: According to the source, describe two ways the branches of power in Tarsa check each other, and explain why power is divided.
source: The constitution of the Republic of Tarsa divides the power of the state into three branches. The parliament, whose members are elected by citizens every five years, makes the laws and approves the national budget. The government, led by a prime minister, carries out the laws and runs public services such as schools and hospitals. The courts decide whether laws have been broken and settle disputes between citizens. Judges cannot be removed by the government, so they can rule freely. Each branch can check the others. Parliament can question ministers and can remove the government by a vote of no confidence. The highest court can cancel a law if it goes against the constitution. The writers of the constitution believed that no single person or group should hold all the power.
points: Parliament can question ministers and remove the government by a vote of no confidence
The highest court can cancel a law that goes against the constitution (and judges cannot be removed by the government)
Power is divided so that no single person or group holds all the power
model_answer: In Tarsa, parliament checks the government because it can question ministers and remove the government with a vote of no confidence. The highest court checks parliament because it can cancel a law that goes against the constitution, and judges cannot be removed by the government. Power is divided because the writers of the constitution believed that no single person or group should hold all the power.

stem: Using Mona's map in the source, in which direction is the school from her house, and how far does she walk to school?
source: Mona drew a map of her neighbourhood for a school project. At the top of the map she drew an arrow with the letter N to show north. Her house is in the middle of the map. The school is north of her house, and the mosque is east of it, next to a small park. The bakery is south of the house, on the corner of Tahrir Street. Mona also added a scale: one centimetre on the map is 100 metres in real life. On the map, the school is 5 centimetres away from her house, so Mona knows that she walks 500 metres to school every morning. She used blue for the canal, green for the park and red for the main roads.
points: The school is north of her house
She walks 500 metres (5 cm on the map, with 1 cm = 100 m)
model_answer: The school is north of Mona's house. It is 5 centimetres away on the map, and 1 centimetre is 100 metres, so she walks 500 metres to school.

stem: Using the source, write a short paragraph (4-8 sentences) describing daily life for the workers of Deir el-Medina.
source: Deir el-Medina was a village in ancient Egypt, near the Valley of the Kings at Thebes. It was home to the skilled workers who cut and decorated the royal tombs. About seventy families lived there, inside a wall. The houses were long and narrow, with a front room, a living room, a small bedroom and a kitchen at the back with an oven for bread. The workers walked up a mountain path to the valley and stayed there for eight days, then came home for two days of rest. They were paid in grain, fish, vegetables, oil and clothing, not in coins. Many workers could read and write. They wrote notes, letters and even complaints on pieces of pottery and stone. One note tells us that when food did not arrive, the workers stopped work and protested.
points: They were skilled workers who cut and decorated the royal tombs and lived with about seventy families in a walled village of long, narrow houses
They worked eight days in the Valley of the Kings, then came home for two days of rest
They were paid in goods such as grain, fish, vegetables, oil and clothing, not coins
Many could read and write; they wrote notes and complaints on pottery and once stopped work to protest when food did not arrive
model_answer: Deir el-Medina was the village of the skilled workers who cut and decorated the royal tombs in the Valley of the Kings. About seventy families lived there inside a wall, in long, narrow houses with a kitchen and bread oven at the back. The workers walked up a mountain path to the valley, worked there for eight days and then came home for two days of rest. They were not paid in coins but in grain, fish, vegetables, oil and clothing. Many of them could read and write, and they wrote notes and complaints on pieces of pottery. Once, when their food did not arrive, they stopped work and protested. Their life was hard, but they were skilled and proud workers.

stem: Using the source, write a paragraph (4-8 sentences) on the advantages and disadvantages of the Aswan High Dam. Give at least two of each and end with a short conclusion.
source: The Aswan High Dam was completed in 1970 across the Nile in southern Egypt. Behind it, a huge reservoir called Lake Nasser formed. The dam brought important benefits. It stopped the yearly flood, so villages and fields were protected from damage. Water stored in the lake could be released all year, which allowed farmers to grow two or even three crops a year instead of one. The dam's turbines produced a large share of Egypt's electricity at the time. However, there were also costs. More than 100,000 Nubian people had to leave their homes, which were flooded by the lake. The fertile silt that the flood used to bring was now trapped behind the dam, so farmers had to buy chemical fertilisers. The ancient temples of Abu Simbel had to be cut into blocks and moved to higher ground.
points: Advantage: it stopped the yearly flood, protecting villages and fields
Advantage: stored water allowed two or three crops a year, and/or its turbines produced much of Egypt's electricity
Disadvantage: more than 100,000 Nubians had to leave homes flooded by Lake Nasser
Disadvantage: the silt was trapped behind the dam, so farmers had to buy chemical fertilisers
model_answer: The Aswan High Dam, completed in 1970, brought Egypt both benefits and costs. On the positive side, it stopped the yearly flood, so villages and fields were protected. Water stored in Lake Nasser could be released all year, letting farmers grow two or three crops a year, and the dam produced a large share of Egypt's electricity. On the negative side, more than 100,000 Nubians had to leave their homes when the lake flooded them. Also, the fertile silt was trapped behind the dam, so farmers had to buy chemical fertilisers. In conclusion, the dam helped farming and energy a great deal, but some people and the land paid a price.

stem: Using the source, write an essay (4-8 sentences) explaining why the Industrial Revolution started in Britain and how it changed people's lives.
source: The Industrial Revolution began in Britain in the second half of the eighteenth century. Several things made Britain a good place for it to start. The country had large amounts of coal and iron under the ground. Its colonies and trade brought raw materials such as cotton and gave merchants money to invest. New machines, such as the spinning jenny, made cloth much faster than people could by hand, and James Watt's improved steam engine could power whole factories. As factories grew, millions of people moved from villages to towns. Life there was hard. Families lived in crowded houses with dirty water, and diseases such as cholera spread quickly. Children as young as six worked long hours in factories and mines. Over time, new laws limited children's working hours, and cities built sewers and clean water supplies.
points: Britain had large amounts of coal and iron
Colonies and trade brought raw materials such as cotton and money to invest
New machines such as the spinning jenny and Watt's steam engine made production faster and powered factories
Millions moved from villages to towns, where crowded houses, dirty water and diseases such as cholera made life hard
Children as young as six worked long hours in factories and mines (later laws limited their hours)
model_answer: The Industrial Revolution began in Britain in the late eighteenth century for several reasons. Britain had large amounts of coal and iron, and its colonies and trade supplied raw materials such as cotton and money to invest. New machines like the spinning jenny made cloth quickly, and James Watt's steam engine could power whole factories. These changes transformed people's lives, as millions moved from villages to towns. There, families lived in crowded houses with dirty water, and diseases like cholera spread fast. Children as young as six worked long hours in factories and mines. Over time, new laws and clean water supplies improved conditions, but the early years were very hard.

stem: Using the source, write 4-8 sentences about the recycling project at Nour Primary School: what the pupils did and what the results were.
source: Pupils at Nour Primary School noticed that the playground was full of plastic bottles and juice boxes after every break. Their class decided to start a recycling project. First, they put three coloured bins in the playground: blue for plastic, yellow for paper and green for food waste. Next, they made posters to explain which rubbish goes in which bin. Every Thursday two pupils from each class check the bins and help younger children. A local company buys the plastic bottles, and the money is used to buy books for the school library. After three months the playground was much cleaner, and the school had sold more than 2,000 bottles. The head teacher said the project taught pupils that small actions by citizens can improve their community.
points: They put three coloured bins in the playground (blue for plastic, yellow for paper, green for food waste)
They made posters explaining which rubbish goes where, and pupils check the bins every Thursday and help younger children
Results: the playground became much cleaner and money from selling the bottles buys library books
model_answer: The pupils of Nour Primary School started a recycling project because their playground was full of bottles and juice boxes. First, they put three coloured bins in the playground: blue for plastic, yellow for paper and green for food waste. Then they made posters to show which rubbish goes in each bin. Every Thursday two pupils from each class check the bins and help the younger children. After three months the playground was much cleaner, and the money from selling more than 2,000 bottles bought books for the library. The project showed that small actions can improve a community.

stem: Using the source, write a paragraph (4-8 sentences) describing Hatshepsut's expedition to Punt and explaining why we know so much about it.
source: Hatshepsut was one of the few women to rule ancient Egypt as pharaoh, around 3,500 years ago. Instead of fighting many wars, she focused on trade and building. Her most famous trade mission was an expedition to the land of Punt, which was probably on the coast of East Africa. Five large ships sailed down the Red Sea. The Egyptians carried gifts such as jewellery, tools and weapons. They returned with gold, ebony wood, animal skins, live baboons and, most importantly, myrrh and frankincense trees. These trees produced sweet-smelling resin that was burned in temples. Hatshepsut was so proud of the expedition that she had its story carved on the walls of her temple at Deir el-Bahari. Thanks to these carvings, we know what the ships, the people of Punt and their houses looked like.
points: Five large ships sailed down the Red Sea to Punt, probably on the coast of East Africa
The Egyptians took gifts such as jewellery, tools and weapons
They brought back gold, ebony, animal skins, baboons and especially myrrh and frankincense trees for temple resin
The story was carved on the walls of her temple at Deir el-Bahari, so we know what the ships, people and houses looked like
model_answer: Hatshepsut, one of the few women to rule Egypt as pharaoh, preferred trade to war. Her most famous mission was an expedition to Punt, probably on the coast of East Africa. Five large ships sailed down the Red Sea carrying gifts such as jewellery, tools and weapons. They returned with gold, ebony, animal skins, live baboons and, most importantly, myrrh and frankincense trees, whose resin was burned in temples. Hatshepsut was so proud that she had the story carved on the walls of her temple at Deir el-Bahari. Thanks to these carvings, we know what the ships, the people of Punt and their houses looked like.

stem: Using the source, write an essay (4-8 sentences) explaining the causes and results of the 1919 Revolution in Egypt.
source: At the end of the First World War, many Egyptians hoped that Britain, which had controlled Egypt since 1882, would allow the country to become independent. In November 1918 a group of Egyptian leaders led by Saad Zaghloul asked to travel to the peace conference in Paris to present Egypt's case. Britain refused. In March 1919 the British arrested Zaghloul and sent him into exile on the island of Malta. News of the arrest led to strikes and demonstrations across the country. Students, workers, lawyers, farmers and women all took part, and Muslims and Christians marched together under one flag. Britain responded with force, and hundreds of Egyptians were killed. In the end Zaghloul was released, and in 1922 Britain declared Egypt independent, although it kept control over defence, the Suez Canal and Sudan.
points: Egyptians wanted independence after the First World War, and Britain refused to let Zaghloul's group go to the Paris peace conference
The arrest of Saad Zaghloul and his exile to Malta in March 1919 led to strikes and demonstrations
People from all groups took part: students, workers, lawyers, farmers, women, Muslims and Christians together
Results: Zaghloul was released and in 1922 Britain declared Egypt independent but kept control of defence, the Suez Canal and Sudan
model_answer: After the First World War, many Egyptians hoped Britain would let Egypt become independent. When Saad Zaghloul and other leaders asked to present Egypt's case at the Paris peace conference, Britain refused. In March 1919 the British arrested Zaghloul and exiled him to Malta, and the news led to strikes and demonstrations across the country. Students, workers, lawyers, farmers and women took part, and Muslims and Christians marched together under one flag. Britain used force and hundreds of Egyptians were killed. In the end Zaghloul was released, and in 1922 Britain declared Egypt independent, although it kept control of defence, the Suez Canal and Sudan. So the revolution won independence, but only a limited one.

stem: Using the source, write 4-8 sentences describing how Marsa Zarqa has changed and what is being done to protect its environment.
source: Marsa Zarqa is a town on the Red Sea coast. Fifty years ago it was a small fishing village of about 2,000 people. Then divers discovered that its coral reefs were full of colourful fish, and hotels began to open along the beach. Today about 40,000 people live there, and most of them work in tourism, in hotels, restaurants, diving centres and transport. A new airport brings visitors from Europe. Tourism has brought jobs and better roads, but it has also caused problems. Some reefs have been damaged by boat anchors and by divers who touch the coral. Hotels use large amounts of fresh water, which must be made from seawater at high cost. To protect the reefs, the town now limits the number of boats and has fixed mooring buoys so that boats do not need to drop anchors.
points: It grew from a fishing village of about 2,000 people to a town of about 40,000 because of tourism (coral reefs, hotels, airport)
Tourism brought jobs and better roads, and most people now work in tourism
Problems: reefs damaged by anchors and by divers touching coral, and hotels use much fresh water made from seawater at high cost
Protection: the town limits the number of boats and has fixed mooring buoys so boats do not drop anchors
model_answer: Fifty years ago Marsa Zarqa was a small fishing village of about 2,000 people, but after divers discovered its colourful coral reefs, hotels opened and a new airport was built. Today about 40,000 people live there, and most of them work in tourism, which has also brought better roads. However, tourism has caused problems. Boat anchors and divers who touch the coral have damaged some reefs, and hotels use large amounts of fresh water made from seawater at high cost. To protect the reefs, the town now limits the number of boats and has fixed mooring buoys so boats do not need to drop anchors. In this way the town is trying to keep both its tourists and its reefs.

stem: Using the source, write an essay (4-8 sentences) explaining how elections in Velmora are organised to be free and fair.
source: In the country of Velmora, every citizen aged eighteen or over has the right to vote. Before an election, citizens must register on the voters' list using their national identity card. On election day, each voter goes to a polling station near home. The voter shows the identity card, receives a ballot paper and goes alone behind a screen to mark it. This secret ballot protects voters from pressure, because nobody can see their choice. After voting, the voter's finger is marked with ink that lasts several days, so that nobody can vote twice. When the polls close, the votes are counted in front of observers from different parties and independent groups. An independent election commission, not the government, announces the results. Citizens who think rules were broken can complain to the courts.
points: Every citizen aged eighteen or over can vote after registering on the voters' list with a national identity card
The secret ballot behind a screen protects voters from pressure
Ink on the finger stops anyone from voting twice
Votes are counted in front of observers from different parties and independent groups
An independent election commission, not the government, announces the results, and complaints can go to the courts
model_answer: Elections in Velmora are organised carefully to be free and fair. Every citizen aged eighteen or over can vote, but must first register on the voters' list with a national identity card. On election day, each voter marks the ballot alone behind a screen, so the secret ballot protects them from pressure. Afterwards their finger is marked with ink so that nobody can vote twice. The votes are counted in front of observers from different parties and independent groups, and an independent commission, not the government, announces the results. Finally, citizens who think the rules were broken can complain to the courts. All these steps help people trust the result.

stem: Using the source, write 4-8 sentences about the date palms of Ain Zahra: why they grow well there and how people use them.

stem: Using the source, write an essay (4-8 sentences) explaining why the Western Roman Empire fell.
source: In the fourth and fifth centuries AD, the Western Roman Empire grew weaker. Historians point to several causes. The empire was enormous, and it was hard to defend its long borders along the Rhine and Danube rivers. Germanic peoples such as the Goths and Vandals crossed these borders, some fleeing the Huns from the east. To pay the army, emperors raised taxes, and many farmers and traders became poor. Rulers changed very often; some emperors ruled only a few months before being killed. In 395 the empire was divided into a western half ruled from Rome and later Ravenna, and an eastern half ruled from Constantinople. The eastern half was richer and survived for another thousand years. In 476 a Germanic commander removed the last western emperor, Romulus Augustulus.
points: The empire was enormous and its long borders along the Rhine and Danube were hard to defend
Germanic peoples such as the Goths and Vandals crossed the borders, some fleeing the Huns
Emperors raised taxes to pay the army, so many farmers and traders became poor
Rulers changed very often and some were killed after a few months
model_answer: The Western Roman Empire fell for several connected reasons. First, the empire was enormous, and its long borders along the Rhine and Danube were hard to defend. Germanic peoples such as the Goths and Vandals crossed these borders, some of them fleeing the Huns. To pay the army, emperors raised taxes, and many farmers and traders became poor. At the same time rulers changed very often, and some emperors were killed after only a few months. While the richer eastern half survived, the west grew weaker until, in 476, a Germanic commander removed the last western emperor. In short, outside attacks and problems inside the empire together brought it down.

stem: Using the source, write 4-8 sentences describing the Library of Alexandria: who built it, how it collected books, and why it declined.
source: The city of Alexandria was founded by Alexander the Great in 331 BC. After his death, Egypt was ruled by the Ptolemy family, who wanted their capital to be the greatest centre of learning in the world. They built the Library of Alexandria, part of a research centre called the Mouseion. The library tried to collect a copy of every book in the world. Ships that came into the harbour were searched for scrolls, which were copied; often the library kept the original and gave back the copy. Scholars from many lands came to study there. Eratosthenes, a head of the library, calculated the size of the Earth with surprising accuracy. Over the centuries the library slowly declined, partly because of fires and wars and because rulers stopped paying for it.
points: It was built by the Ptolemy rulers, who wanted Alexandria to be the greatest centre of learning
It tried to collect every book: ships in the harbour were searched and scrolls copied, often keeping the originals
Scholars came from many lands; for example Eratosthenes calculated the size of the Earth
It declined slowly because of fires, wars and rulers no longer paying for it
model_answer: The Library of Alexandria was built by the Ptolemy family, who ruled Egypt after Alexander the Great and wanted Alexandria to be the greatest centre of learning in the world. It tried to collect a copy of every book. Ships arriving in the harbour were searched for scrolls, which were copied, and the library often kept the originals. Scholars came from many lands, and Eratosthenes, one of its heads, calculated the size of the Earth. Over the centuries the library slowly declined because of fires and wars and because rulers stopped paying for it. Even so, it is remembered as a great centre of knowledge.

stem: Using the source, write an essay (4-8 sentences) explaining the causes of desertification in the Sahel and how people are fighting it.
source: The Sahel is a long strip of dry grassland south of the Sahara Desert. In many parts of the Sahel, land that was once used for farming and grazing is turning into desert. This process is called desertification. It has natural and human causes. Rainfall in the region varies greatly, and long droughts have become more frequent. At the same time, the population has grown quickly, so more land is farmed and more animals graze. When too many animals eat the grass, the roots die and the soil is left bare. People also cut trees for firewood. Without plants to hold it, the soil is blown away by wind. Some communities are fighting back. In the Great Green Wall project, countries are planting trees across Africa, and farmers protect young trees that grow naturally in their fields. Simple stone lines across slopes also slow rainwater so that it soaks into the soil.
points: Natural cause: rainfall varies greatly and long droughts have become more frequent
Population growth means more grazing; too many animals eat the grass, the roots die and the soil is left bare
People cut trees for firewood, and without plants the soil is blown away by wind
People plant trees (the Great Green Wall) and farmers protect young trees growing in their fields
Stone lines across slopes slow rainwater so it soaks into the soil
model_answer: Desertification is the process by which farmland and grazing land in the Sahel turn into desert, and it has both natural and human causes. Naturally, rainfall varies greatly and long droughts have become more frequent. Because the population has grown, more animals graze, and when they eat too much grass the roots die and the soil is left bare. People also cut trees for firewood, so without plants the wind blows the soil away. Communities are fighting back: in the Great Green Wall project countries plant trees across Africa, and farmers protect young trees in their fields. Simple stone lines across slopes also slow rainwater so it soaks into the soil. These efforts show that desertification can be slowed when people work together.

stem: Using the source, write 4-8 sentences explaining how the residents of Al-Zohour Street solved their problems.
source: The residents of Al-Zohour Street were unhappy because rubbish was piling up on the corner and the street lamps were broken. Instead of only complaining, they formed a neighbourhood committee. Twelve neighbours met in the house of Mr Hassan and chose a leader, a secretary and a treasurer. The committee wrote a polite letter to the local council, signed by sixty residents, asking for the lamps to be repaired. They also organised a cleaning day on a Friday morning. Families brought brooms and bags, and young people painted the walls. Each family now pays five pounds a month for a worker who collects the rubbish every day. Two months later, the council repaired the lamps. Mr Hassan said, "When neighbours work together, they can change their street."

They sent the council a polite letter signed by sixty residents, and the council repaired the lamps
They held a cleaning day, and each family now pays five pounds a month for a worker who collects the rubbish

The committee sent a polite letter signed by sixty residents to the local council, and two months later the council repaired the lamps. They also organised a cleaning day on a Friday, and now each family pays five pounds a month for a worker who collects the rubbish every day. As Mr Hassan said, neighbours who work together can change their street.

stem: Using the source, write 4-8 sentences explaining what causes the summer monsoon and how it affects farmers.
source: In South Asia, the year is shaped by the monsoon, a seasonal change in wind direction. In winter, dry winds blow from the land towards the sea, so there is little rain. In summer the land heats up much faster than the Indian Ocean. Warm air rises over the land, and moist winds blow in from the ocean to take its place. As this moist air rises over hills and mountains, it cools and drops heavy rain. Between June and September some places receive most of their rain for the whole year. Farmers depend on the monsoon to water rice and other crops. If the rains arrive late or are weak, crops fail and food prices rise. If the rains are too heavy, rivers overflow and floods destroy homes and fields.
points: In summer the land heats up faster than the ocean and warm air rises over the land
Moist winds blow in from the ocean, and as the air rises over hills and mountains it cools and drops heavy rain
Farmers depend on the monsoon rain to water rice and other crops
Late or weak rains make crops fail and food prices rise, while very heavy rains cause floods that destroy homes and fields
model_answer: The summer monsoon is caused by a seasonal change in wind direction. In summer the land in South Asia heats up much faster than the Indian Ocean, so warm air rises over the land. Moist winds then blow in from the ocean, and as this air rises over hills and mountains it cools and drops heavy rain. Farmers depend on this rain to water their rice and other crops. However, if the rains are late or weak, crops fail and food prices rise. If they are too heavy, rivers overflow and floods destroy homes and fields. So the monsoon can bring both life and danger to farmers.

stem: Using the source, write an essay (4-8 sentences) describing the problem of child labour in Beit Hanna, the council's programme, and how successful it was.
source: In the town of Beit Hanna, a survey found that one child in eight between the ages of ten and fourteen worked instead of going to school, mostly in brick factories and workshops. The town council knew that the country had signed the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, which says that every child has the right to education and to be protected from dangerous work. The council therefore started a programme with three parts. First, poor families receive a small monthly payment if their children attend school regularly. Second, inspectors visit workshops, and owners who employ children under fifteen are fined. Third, the town opened evening classes so that older children who left school can catch up. After two years, the number of working children had fallen by half. However, some families said the payment was too small to replace a child's wages.

The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child gives every child the right to education and protection from dangerous work
Poor families receive a monthly payment if their children attend school regularly
Inspectors fine owners who employ children under fifteen, and evening classes help older children catch up
After two years working children fell by half, but some families said the payment was too small to replace a child's wages
model_answer: In Beit Hanna, a survey showed that one child in eight aged ten to fourteen worked, mostly in brick factories and workshops, instead of going to school. Because the country had signed the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, which gives every child the right to education and protection from dangerous work, the council acted. Its programme had three parts: poor families receive a monthly payment if their children attend school, inspectors fine owners who employ children under fifteen, and evening classes help older children catch up. After two years, the number of working children had fallen by half. However, some families said the payment was too small to replace a child's wages.
